transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I came in because I just... I barely sleep right anymore. It's like my brain won't shut off when I want it to. I'll just lie there in the dark, and if it's raining outside, even just a little drizzle, I hear the water hitting the roof and suddenly I'm wide awake, thinking about the bluff giving way. I can picture the mud and the rocks and everything just coming down. And I'll lie there for hours, just tossing and turning, trying to get comfortable, trying to think about something else, anything else. But it's like a loop in my head. And then, when I finally do pass out, usually because I'm just completely exhausted, it's not even real rest. I'll wake up completely drenched in sweat, my heart pounding, because of these dreams... these awful dreams that just feel so real. And then my alarm goes off, and I have to drag myself out of bed, put on my headset, and show up to the call center feeling like I never even closed my eyes. I mean, I'm talking to angry customers all day about their bills, and I can barely focus because I'm just so drained. It's been happening so much lately, I just don't know how much longer I can keep doing this on like two hours of broken sleep.
Do you find that these thoughts or images, like the bluff giving way, come up even when you don’t want them to and cause you a lot of distress?

Yeah, exactly. It's like... it's like I have no control over it whatsoever. I'll just be sitting there, you know? Like, I'll be at my desk at the call center, right in the middle of explaining a billing cycle to Mrs. Smith or whoever, and then... boom. Stuff just pops in my head out of nowhere. It's not even like I'm trying to think about it, or even that something specific triggered it, it just invades my brain. I'll hear this sound, this awful, grinding sound of rocks sliding, or I'll suddenly feel this pressure, like my leg is stuck under me again and I can't move it, no matter how hard I pull. And for a minute... for a solid minute, I'm not in my cubicle anymore. I'm not wearing my headset. I'm right back out on that trail, in the mud, feeling that panic all over again. And it's terrifying, honestly. It takes me a second to snap back to reality and realize I'm at work, and usually by then the customer is yelling "hello? hello?" in my ear because I just stopped talking mid-sentence. It's so distressing because I never know when it's going to happen, you know? It's like my brain is just waiting to ambush me when I least expect it.
Can you tell me more about what happened on that trail? Were you in any actual danger or did something happen to you during that experience?

Yeah, I mean, I was in a lot of danger. I really thought I was going to die out there. It was... gosh, it was supposed to be just a normal Saturday. I actually had the weekend off from the call center for once, which is rare because they always try to pressure us into picking up overtime shifts, and I just wanted to get out of my apartment, you know? Just get away from the screens and the noise. So I went up to this trail I've been to like a hundred times. It's this path that cuts right along the edge of a steep bluff. It had been raining a ton that whole week, but it was just sort of drizzling that morning, so I really didn't think anything of it. 

I remember the mud was super thick that day. It was caking onto the bottom of my boots, making them feel like they weighed ten pounds each, and I was just looking down, trying not to slip. And then... I felt the ground literally just drop out from under my left foot. I didn't even have a second to react. I just heard this sickening crack, and then this deep, horrible rumbling sound. It wasn't like in the movies where you have time to jump out of the way or grab onto a branch. The entire side of the bluff just gave way. 

I slid down the ravine, I don't even know how far, maybe twenty or thirty feet, just tumbling with all this heavy, wet earth and these massive, jagged rocks. And when I finally stopped sliding, everything was completely silent for a second, except for the rain hitting my jacket. I thought I was okay, but then I tried to sit up and move, and I couldn't. This huge rock—it must have been a couple hundred pounds at least—had slid right on top of my leg, pinning it deep in the mud. I was completely trapped. I was yanking at my leg, tearing my fingernails up trying to dig the mud out from under the rock, but it was like wet concrete. The water was rushing down the hill around me, washing more dirt down onto me, and I was absolutely terrified that the rest of the cliff was going to come down and just bury me alive before anyone even knew I was missing. I was stuck out there in the freezing rain for almost four hours, just screaming until my throat bled, before another hiker finally heard me. So, yeah... it was bad. I can still feel exactly how heavy that rock was.
Since that experience on the trail, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, sounds, or situations that remind you of what happened?

Well, yeah, definitely. I mean, I absolutely will not go anywhere near the coast trails now. Not a chance. Even just thinking about driving out toward that side of town, where you can smell the salt in the air and see the trees starting to get thicker... it just makes me feel sick to my stomach. I used to love it out there, you know? It was my escape. But now, if I even see a picture of a trail that looks remotely like it on Instagram or something, I have to scroll past it instantly. I can't even look at it. 

And it's not just the places, it's the people too. My hiking buddies, the guys I used to go out with every other weekend, they've been texting me non-stop. 'Hey man, you want to hit the gorge this Saturday?' 'Hey, weather's supposed to be great, let's do the ridge.' And I just... I dodge them. I leave them on read, or I make up some excuse about having to pick up an extra shift at the call center, which is a lie because I can barely handle the hours I have now. But I just can't face them. Because I know if I text them back, they're going to want to talk about going out there, and even just the thought of talking about hiking, about putting on my boots and stepping onto dirt... my chest just tightens up so bad. It feels like someone is sitting on my ribs and I can't catch a full breath. I feel terrible because they're good guys and they don't understand why I'm ghosting them, but I just can't bring myself to even have a conversation about it. It's like my whole body just rejects the idea of anything related to that day.
